plain_english: Here's what real devotion to the gods means: think correctly about them. They exist. They run the universe fairly and well. Commit to obeying them, giving in to them, and following them willingly through whatever happens. They rule with perfect wisdom. If you do this, you'll never blame the gods or accuse them of abandoning you.
original_excerpt: Be assured that the essence of piety toward the gods lies in this—to form right opinions concerning them, as existing and as governing the universe justly and well. And fix yourself in this resolution, to obey them, and yield to them, and willingly follow them amidst all events, as being ruled by the most perfect wisdom. For thus you will never find fault with the gods, nor accuse them of neglecting you.

plain_english: There's only one way to achieve this: stop caring about things you can't control. Only call things good or bad if they're actually up to you. If you think other things are good or bad, you'll inevitably get upset when you don't get what you want or when bad things happen. Then you'll blame whoever caused it.
original_excerpt: And it is not possible for this to be affected in any other way than by withdrawing yourself from things which are not within our own power, and by making good or evil to consist only in those which are. For if you suppose any other things to be either good or evil, it is inevitable that, when you are disappointed of what you wish or incur what you would avoid, you should reproach and blame their authors.

plain_english: Every living thing naturally runs from what seems harmful and chases after what seems good. So it's impossible for someone who thinks they're being hurt to feel happy about the person hurting them. You can't enjoy the hurt itself either. This is why a father gets cursed by his son when he doesn't give him what the son thinks is good. It's why Polynices and Eteocles became enemies — they both thought ruling the empire was good. This is why farmers curse the gods, and sailors do too, and merchants, and people who lose their spouse or children.
original_excerpt: For every creature is naturally formed to flee and abhor things that appear hurtful and that which causes them; and to pursue and admire those which appear beneficial and that which causes them. It is impracticable, then, that one who supposes himself to be hurt should rejoice in the person who, as he thinks, hurts him, just as it is impossible to rejoice in the hurt itself. Hence, also, a father is reviled by his son when he does not impart the things which seem to be good; and this made Polynices and Eteocles mutually enemies—that empire seemed good to both. On this account the husbandman reviles the gods; [and so do] the sailor, the merchant, or those who have lost wife or child.

plain_english: Your devotion follows your priorities. If you properly control what you want and what you avoid, you'll naturally care about being devout too. But everyone should also make offerings, sacrifices, and give first fruits according to their country's customs. Do this sincerely — not carelessly or lazily, not cheaply, and not wastefully either.
original_excerpt: For where our interest is, there, too, is piety directed. So that whoever is careful to regulate his desires and aversions as he ought is thus made careful of piety likewise. But it also becomes incumbent on everyone to offer libations and sacrifices and first fruits, according to the customs of his country, purely, and not heedlessly nor negligently; not avariciously, nor yet extravagantly.
